claim as made in prose: On 3 October 2013 Adobe's CSO wrote that attackers had accessed Adobe customer IDs and encrypted passwords
Adobe recommended changing the password on any site where the same one was used
The old database was kept as a backup measure in case of issues with the new system
The grouping-by-ciphertext-then-hints route is what OPC para 17 and DPC describe; no decryption on the record
Attackers identified and removed data from a backup server
DPC: research articles showed some passwords deciphered by reference to hints and repeated passwords
DPC: the transition could have been achieved more effectively and expeditiously
DPC: hints were those of a small percentage of users; no report says the key was recovered
source: irish-dpc-2014-adobe.txt, Hints (absence of key-recovery claim checked across all three excerpts)

claim as made in prose: DPC queried encrypted vs hashed; Adobe said it had hashed and salted in a new system for years but kept the old database as a backup
DPC satisfied Adobe now has appropriate procedures in place
HIBP: 153 million accounts, each with a plain-text hint; cryptography poorly done, many resolved to plain text
Wikipedia, quoting LastPass: Adobe failed to use best practices and has not salted them
WIRED: 6.5 million hashed (encrypted) LinkedIn passwords, 300,000 decrypted and posted
Harsha et al.: over 177.5+ million unsalted SHA-1 hashes stolen in 2012
Harsha et al.: unsalted SHA-1 hashes; no key stretching such as PBKDF2 or Argon2; significantly easier to crack
The available record does not say the hashed store was taken; the Irish and Australian reports identify the compromised data as coming from the backup system
source: irish-dpc-2014-adobe.txt How the Breach Occurred; australia-oaic-adobe-extended.txt Background

claim as made in prose: LinkedIn became aware on 6 June 2012 of the theft of approximately 6.5 million passwords
May 2016: 2012 data resurfaced; emails, hashed passwords, member IDs; not a new breach; salted hashes and optional 2FA now
LinkedIn completed a long-planned transition from hashed to hashed-and-salted passwords
Adobe introduced a replacement authentication system in April 2010
Adobe's new system: SHA-256, salted, iterated more than 1,000 times
NIST: verifiers shall not permit a hint accessible to an unauthenticated claimant
NIST: salt prevents accounts sharing the same hash; cost factor makes each guess more expensive, guessing attack high or prohibitive
OAIC: encryption plus hints let experts identify the 100 most common passwords and associated accounts; database widely available online
Triple DES; same ciphertext for common shared passwords; hints stored in plain text
The attacker took a copy of a backup database containing usernames, emails, encrypted passwords, plain-text hints, names, addresses, encrypted card numbers
1,787,100 Australians current password data; 218,750 obsolete; 36 plain text; 135,288 payment
Current password data means a password valid against Adobe's production authentication system
OAIC: the attacker compromised a public-facing web server and used it to access other Adobe servers; the report does not identify how that server was compromised
OAIC: breach of NPP 4; measures in one area do not satisfy NPP 4 if not applied to all personal information
source: australia-oaic-adobe-extended.txt NPP 4 conclusion; australia-oaic-adobe.txt NPP 4 paragraph

claim as made in prose: OAIC: new system introduced April 2010; SHA-256, salted, iterated more than 1,000 times
OAIC lists network monitoring, storage changes, two-factor, decommissioning the affected server, abolishing hints
Passwords reset on 3-4 October 2013 for users whose current password data was in the database
OAIC: common passwords shared by different users had the same ciphertext representation
Access 30 Aug-17 Sep 2013; discovered 17 Sep via an attempt to decrypt card numbers; reported 3 Oct
Adobe estimated over one million Canadian customers affected; same data types listed
OPC concerns: password management, outdated software, redundant systems, logging, retention, network isolation
OPC: safeguards not appropriate; complaint well-founded and resolved
OPC: some systems inherited from absorbed companies contributed to the problems
Adobe described a sophisticated, long-term intrusion
OPC lists password-management and authentication enhancements, decommissioning the affected server, reduced retention; many measures confidential
OPC: hints sometimes contained the password; format scrambled identical passwords the same way; easy to reach several accounts from one hint
Stajano et al.: reversibly encrypted with 3DES, not salted and hashed, in ECB mode
Stajano: with salt attackers cannot tell who shares a password, but can still try likely guesses
Credential data remained reachable on the backup system more than three years after the replacement system was introduced (April 2010 to the Aug-Sep 2013 intrusion)
source: australia-oaic-adobe-extended.txt, Background and Security of Passwords (arithmetic on the two dates)
